rows.evidence: jama_rathinam_2019_oi_190092.pdf PDF p. 3 (Figure 1, rendered), p. 6 (Table 2, rendered), p. 7 (12-month outcomes text).

Figure 1 12-month boxes: MTX failures = 20 switched + 9 unwilling + 3 not eligible (safety) = 32; MMF = 29 + 11 + 2 = 42, so every failure is accounted for. Eligible (non-safety) failures = 29 + 40 = 69; all failures = 74; text says 68. 20 + 29 = 49 reconciles. 20/32 = 62.5%, 29/42 = 69.05% reproduce, but these use all failures, not the 'eligible' denominator (eligible-based: 20/29 = 69.0%, 29/40 = 72.5%). 49/68 = 72.1% vs 49/69 = 71.0%. The final SAP adds only a sensitivity rule.

The article's definition lists inflammation control, steroid dose, and no failure for intolerability or safety, and states that injections after 90 days were 'considered protocol deviations'. Page 6 reports 4 such patients per arm. rows.R: Missed doses 4.6% (SD 1.0, n = 96) vs 4.3% (SD 0.5, n = 98), with P = .87 by Welch t test. A Welch test on these summaries gives t = 2.63, P = .009 (n = 107/108: P = .006). P = .87 would need an SE of about 1.8, roughly 16 times larger. Either the SDs or the P value is wrong, and the reader cannot tell which. The SDs look implausibly small.
rows.evidence: jama_rathinam_2019_oi_190092.pdf PDF p. 6 (Table 2 missed-doses row and text, rendered), p. 4-5 (Statistical Analysis: 'Missed doses were compared by group using a Welch t test').
rows.rationale: scipy.stats.ttest_ind_from_stats(4.6, 1.0, 96, 4.3, 0.5, 98, equal_var=False) -> t = 2.634, P = 0.0094; with n = 107/108, P = 0.0061. Back-solving: P = .87 corresponds to |t| of about 0.164, i.e., an SE of about 1.83 for a 0.3-point difference. Even treating the printed SDs as SEs gives P of about .79, not .87. The text repeats 4.6% (1.0) and 4.3% (0.5) with P = .87. The summaries and the test result are mutually incompatible. Which number is wrong is unknown, so it is confirmed but with no known correct value. I rate it substantive because extracted dispersion (SD) or the adherence inference is unreliable. The 0.3-point mean difference is clinically trivial whichever is right.

rows.R: Table 2, heart failure: 8-year KM incidence 18.9% (control) - 6.8% (surgery) = 12.1, but the ARD is printed 12.9 (CI 10.4-15.1, centred on 12.9). The gap of 0.8 pp exceeds rounding (max about 0.1). The same pattern affects all 5 single nonfatal outcomes, while the composites and mortality reconcile exactly. This suggests a different (unstated) estimator, eg 1-KM vs competing-risk incidence.
rows.evidence: jama_aminian_2019_oi_190103.pdf PDF p. 7 (Table 2, rendered), p. 4 (Statistical Analysis text); joi190103supp1_prod.pdf PDF p. 7 (eTable 5, same incidences).
rows.rationale: Recomputed every Table 2 row (control minus surgery). Primary 47.7-30.8 = 16.9 (printed 16.9); secondary 27.6-17.0 = 10.6 (10.6); mortality 17.8-10.0 = 7.8 (7.8). HF 12.1 vs 12.9; CAD 3.7 vs 4.2; cerebrovascular 1.5 vs 1.8; nephropathy 10.2 vs 11.1; AF 5.7 vs 6.5. The maximum gap from one-decimal rounding of two inputs is 0.1. The bootstrap CIs are centred on the printed ARDs, so the ARD point and CI share one computation and the incidences come from another. Methods say both are from Kaplan-Meier. The discrepant rows are exactly the outcomes subject to the competing risk of death, which is consistent with mixing 1-KM and a competing-risk estimator, but the paper does not say so. The direction and significance of the HF result are unchanged. The ARD is an extractable effect estimate that disagrees with its own components by about 7% of its value, so I rate it substantive with direct extraction impact.

rows.evidence: joi190108supp1_prod.pdf PDF p. 30-31 (sections 5.3-5.4: ARF criteria and reintubation criteria, text layer; title page: Version 4, 17 October 2017); jama_thille_2019_oi_190108.pdf PDF p. 3 (Outcomes, text layer). The workbook gave no location; located myself.

Only protocol version 4 is supplied, so I cannot tell whether a later amendment changed it. The criterion governs a component of the reintubation decision (primary outcome) and the exploratory outcome 'patients meeting reintubation criteria', so I describe it as a substantive difference. That does not establish that outcomes were misclassified. The escalation pattern in the other criteria makes it plausible that the protocol's 7.35 is a copying error.

rows.R: eTable 2, hypercapnic patients: ineffective cough 14/45 (69) and 16/59 (73), but 14/45 = 31.1% and 16/59 = 27.1%. The printed percentages are the complements (31/45 = 68.9%, 43/59 = 72.9%). rows.evidence: joi190108supp2_prod.pdf PDF p. 4 (eTable 2 continuation, rendered); jama_thille_2019_oi_190108.pdf Table 1 (ineffective cough 65/284 (23), 86/322 (27), text layer). The workbook gave no location; located myself.

Because a reader using the percentages would believe that about 70% rather than about 30% of hypercapnic patients had ineffective cough, I rate it substantive for descriptive interpretation, although no trial effect estimate is affected.

rows.R: Nonhypercapnic day-7 reintubation: eTable 4 gives P = .1057, and the main text gives P = .10. Recomputed: uncorrected chi-square on 45/254 vs 35/276 gives P = 0.1057, which rounds to .11 (Figure 3 log-rank also .11). The text truncated rather than rounded. Inference unchanged. I changed E to statistical_results because this is a numeric rounding question.
rows.evidence: jama_thille_2019_oi_190108.pdf PDF p. 7 (Subgroup text, text layer), p. 8 (Figure 3B log-rank P = .11, rendered); joi190108supp2_prod.pdf PDF p. 7 (eTable 4, rendered). The workbook gave no location; located myself.
rows.rationale: scipy chi2_contingency([[45,209],[35,241]], correction=False) gives P = 0.10573, matching eTable 4's .1057. Yates-corrected: 0.135; Fisher: 0.115. Under JAMA's 2-digit convention .1057 should be .11; .10 is truncation. The difference -5.0 (-11.2 to 1.1) matches. A trivial rounding inconsistency for a nonsignificant subgroup result, so minor. Domain changed from the AI's report_internal_inconsistency to statistical_results: the question is whether a reported P value is correctly rounded from a recomputable value, not a conflict of meaning between documents.

rows.R: The protocol addendum (submitted 3/2015) specifies MICE with 10 imputed data sets combined by Rubin's rules; the article reports M = 20 with Rubin's rules. The method is as planned. Doubling M only reduces Monte Carlo error and cannot bias estimates or change interpretation. This is a real but immaterial implementation difference, so I do not retain it.
rows.evidence: joi190122supp1_prod.pdf PDF p. 32 (section 15c, text layer; addendum dated 3/2/2015, implemented 2/24/2016); jama_de_boer_2019_oi_190122.pdf PDF p. 3 (Statistical Analysis).
rows.rationale: Quoted: plan 'Results from 10 imputation datasets will be combined using Rubin's rules'; article 'Multiple imputation (M = 20) was used for missing data ... combined across imputations using Rubin rules'. The imputation model and combining rule are as planned. M = 20 vs 10 changes only between-imputation Monte Carlo precision, in the conservative direction. I judge it not a meaningful planned-versus-reported difference and exclude it (the AI suggested retain). A reviewer recording every numeric deviation descriptively could reasonably retain it with no further judgment. Aside: the plan's ITT definition ('all participants who return at least one follow-up biosample') is narrower than the article's 'regardless of adherence or follow-up'. That is not part of this candidate.

rows.evidence: joi190023supp1_prod.pdf PDF p. 19 (synopsis), p. 25 (Outcome Measures: Tertiary outcome), p. 45 (summary of changes, 2012.12.8); jama_urashima_2019_oi_190023.pdf PDF p. 3 (Outcomes), p. 8 (Table 3).

The article follows the earlier safety framing. The event definition is the same in all documents, and Table 3 gives the by-randomization-group counts that a tertiary-outcome analysis would use. No significance test is presented as an efficacy result. The difference is in endpoint classification, not in conduct or available data, so I describe it as minor presentation. Agree with AI domain.

The text layer shows the same for GA and AA (77/103, 24/38). No CDK2 locus appears in the protocol. A labeling error with recoverable meaning. Minor.

rows.evidence: jama_urashima_2019_oi_190023.pdf PDF p. 2-3 (Intervention and Outcomes, text layer), p. 6-7 (axes 'Years After Randomization'); joi190023supp1_prod.pdf PDF p. 25 and p. 29 (protocol outcome definitions).

The protocol defines RFS/OS from the supplement start day. The article itself equates the two origins, so this is equivalent wording, not a planned-versus-reported difference. Exclude (the AI suggested retain but itself noted the equivalence).

rows.R: Table 2 footnote: 'HR values greater than 1 indicate that vitamin D ... was associated with a decreased probability of the outcome.' Everywhere else, HR < 1 means benefit: relapse 41/251 (16.3%) vs 36/166 (21.7%) with sHR 0.75; text calls middle-subgroup sHR 0.44 'significantly lower'; Figure 3A shows vitamin D below placebo with HR 0.46. The footnote reverses the direction.
rows.evidence: jama_urashima_2019_oi_190023.pdf PDF p. 7 (Table 2 footnote a and Figure 3, rendered), p. 6 (competing-risk text), p. 4 (event counts).
rows.rationale: Crude proportions: relapse 41/251 = 16.3% vs 36/166 = 21.7%, paired with sHR 0.75; noncancer death 10/251 = 4.0% vs 9/166 = 5.4%, HR 0.70; cancer-specific death 27/251 = 10.8% vs 16/166 = 9.6%, HR 1.09. These are crude diagnostics, not reproductions of the HRs, but every direction is consistent with HR < 1 favoring vitamin D. The text and Figures 2-3 use the same orientation. The footnote states the opposite. A reader relying on Table 2 alone (it contains the subgroup and cause-specific estimates) would invert the direction of effect, for example reading sHR 0.44 in the 20-40 ng/mL subgroup as harm. I rate this a substantive inconsistency because it concerns the direction of reported effect estimates, even though the text allows correction.

rows.R: eTable 5 (per protocol), Women/Quantitative/10.2: the PPV-difference point estimate is printed as '-' while the arm PPVs (15.9, 34.1) and CI [-34.7, -1.3] are shown. From eTable 4: 11/69 = 15.9%, 14/41 = 34.1%, difference -18.2 pp. All three women rows (the only negative two-digit values) lost their magnitude, which suggests column clipping. Recoverable, but missing.

rows.R: DIC: 1/989 vs 0/987 with RR 2.00 (1.91-2.09) and P > .99. A high-vs-low RR is undefined with 0 events, and a CI excluding 1 contradicts P > .99. 2.00 equals the high-PEEP risk divided by the pooled risk: (1/989)/(1/1976) = 2.00. That ratio also reproduces many Table 3 RRs (pleural effusion 1.34, crude 2.04; mortality 1.41, crude 2.40). The whole RR column needs checking.
rows.evidence: jama_bluth_2019_oi_190055_16092.pdf PDF p. 9-10 (Table 3 and footnotes, p. 9 rendered), p. 4-5 (Statistical Analysis, text layer).
rows.rationale: Methods state that RRs and CIs were 'calculated using the Wald likelihood ratio approximation test' with no zero-cell rule. With b = 0 the crude RR is infinite. A 0.5 continuity correction gives about 3.0 with a CI spanning orders of magnitude, so neither 2.00 nor a CI of 1.91-2.09 is attainable, and a CI excluding 1 cannot coexist with P > .99. Exploratory check (my own computation, not claimed by the AI): risk_high/pooled_risk reproduces the printed RR to within 0.01 for most rows, including aspiration (1.33 vs crude 2.00), ARDS (1.50 vs 2.99), pneumothorax (0.50 vs 0.33), edema (1.31 vs 1.89), mortality (1.41 vs 2.40) and pleural effusion (1.34 vs 1.35 printed; crude 2.04). It does not for some common outcomes (primary 0.95 vs printed 0.93, crude 0.90; hypotension 1.29 vs 1.43, crude 1.84). The CIs are also narrower than the counts support (primary: printed 0.83-1.04; crude Wald 0.77-1.07). The DIC row is confirmed as an issue. The pattern suggests the RR column may not compare high vs low PEEP, which would be substantive for every secondary RR. That broader claim needs verification against the analysis code.
